title: Take-on-Exercise2
text:
This prototype focuses on the clustering module of the proposed Shiny application. The goal of the module is to segment customers into behaviorally distinct groups by combining customer-level attributes with transaction-derived features. The analysis uses two related datasets: a customer-level table containing demographic, product, satisfaction, and service variables, and a transaction-level table containing detailed transaction records. By integrating these two sources, the clustering workflow is able to move beyond simple demographic profiling and capture richer patterns of customer behavior.

library(tidyverse)
library(skimr)
library(janitor)
library(lubridate)
library(cluster)
library(factoextra)
library(corrplot)
library(GGally)
library(patchwork)
library(scales)
library(plotly)
library(DT)

Then we analyse monthly fluctuations characterize to check the stability of customer.Customer activity stability differs widely across the user base

  mutate(month = floor_date(date, "month")) %>%
  group_by(customer_id, month) %>%
  summarise(
    monthly_n = n(),
    monthly_amount = sum(amount, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

    monthly_amount_sd = sd(monthly_amount, na.rm = TRUE),
    monthly_n_mean = mean(monthly_n, na.rm = TRUE),

text:
4 Conclusion
This clustering module demonstrates that meaningful customer segmentation can be achieved by combining customer-level attributes with transaction-derived behavioral features. The final k=3 solution identifies three interpretable segments: Low-Engagement Basic Users, At-Risk Active Users, and High-Value Power Users. These segments differ not only in transaction behavior and monetary value, but also in feature usage diversity, support interaction, satisfaction, and churn risk. As a prototype module for the final Shiny application, this clustering workflow provides a strong foundation for interactive exploration of customer heterogeneity and for linking behavioral segments with downstream predictive analysis.

title: Take-on-Exercise2
text:
5.UI Design
The proposed Shiny UI for the clustering module should support both overview and drill-down analysis. On the input side, users should be able to select the profiling metric of interest, switch between visualization modes, and optionally filter by customer characteristics such as segment or acquisition channel. On the output side, the module should provide:
(1) a cluster size summary chart,
(2) a PCA projection plot for structural overview,
(3) a standardized profile heatmap for segment comparison,
(4) boxplots for selected key indicators such as transaction count, transaction amount, and customer lifetime value, and
(5) a summary table describing the characteristics of each segment.
This design would allow end users to understand not only how large each customer segment is, but also how the segments differ in engagement, value, and risk.

       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(              
    aes(data_id = ID),              
    stackgroups = TRUE,                  
    binwidth = 1,                        
    method = "histodot") +  
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0,100)) + 
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,

  geom_dotplot_interactive(              
    aes(data_id = ID),              
    stackgroups = TRUE,                  
    binwidth = 1,                        
    method = "histodot") + 
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0,100)) + 
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,               
                     breaks = NULL)

       width_svg = 6,
       height_svg = 3,
       options = list(
         opts_hover(css = "fill: #202020;"),
         opts_hover_inv(css = "opacity:0.2;")
         )

        x = ~ENGLISH, 
        y = ~MATHS,

Standard scatter plots only show two variables. Comparing Math vs. English and Math vs. Science separately loses the connection between the same student.

p1 <- ggplot(data=d, 
            aes(x = MATHS,
                y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point(size=1) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0,100),
                  ylim=c(0,100))

            aes(x = MATHS,
                y = SCIENCE)) +
  geom_point(size=1) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0,100),
                  ylim=c(0,100))
subplot(ggplotly(p1),
        ggplotly(p2))

DT::datatable(exam_data, class= "compact")







3.8.2 Linked brushing: crosstalk method
The results indicate a clear positive correlation between Mathematics and English scores. Through the interactive hover effect, I identified several outliers in Class 3C who performed exceptionally well in Math but poorly in English. The interactive visualization successfully highlighted these anomalies that were hidden in dense clusters of a static scatter plot. By using linked views with a data table, I could immediately identify the IDs of these students, providing a multi-dimensional insight into individual learning gaps

17.5 Plotting Cycle Plot
In this section, you will learn how to plot a cycle plot showing the time-series patterns and trend of visitor arrivals from Vietnam programmatically by using ggplot2 functions.

17.5.1 Step 1: Data Import
For the purpose of this hands-on exercise, arrivals_by_air.xlsx will be used.
The code chunk below imports arrivals_by_air.xlsx by using read_excel() of readxl package and save it as a tibble data frame called air.


17.5.2 Step 2: Deriving month and year fields
Next, two new fields called month and year are derived from Month-Year field.

air <- read_excel("data/arrivals_by_air.xlsx")
air$month <- factor(month(air$`Month-Year`), 
                    levels=1:12, 
                    labels=month.abb, 
                    ordered=TRUE) 
air$year <- year(ymd(air$`Month-Year`))



17.5.3 Step 4: Extracting the target country
Next, the code chunk below is use to extract data for the target country (i.e. Vietnam)

Vietnam <- air %>% 
  select(`Vietnam`, 
         month, 
         year) %>%
  filter(year >= 2010)



17.5.4 Step 5: Computing year average arrivals by month
The code chunk below uses group_by() and summarise() of dplyr to compute year average arrivals by month.

hline.data <- Vietnam %>% 
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(avgvalue = mean(`Vietnam`))



17.5.5 Srep 6: Plotting the cycle plot
The code chunk below is used to plot the cycle plot as shown in Slide 12/23.

ggplot() + 
  geom_line(data=Vietnam,
            aes(x=year, 
                y=`Vietnam`, 
                group=month), 
            colour="black") +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept=avgvalue), 
             data=hline.data, 
             linetype=6, 
             colour="red", 
             size=0.5) + 
  facet_grid(~month) +
  labs(axis.text.x = element_blank(),
       title = "Visitor arrivals from Vietnam by air, Jan 2010-Dec 2019") +
  xlab("") +
  ylab("No. of Visitors") +
  theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica")

rice <- read_csv("data/rice.csv")

library(CGPfunctions)

               plotly, gganimate, tidyverse)


col <- c("Country", "Continent")
globalPop <- read_xls("data/GlobalPopulation.xls",
                      sheet="Data") %>%
  mutate_at(col, as.factor) %>%
  mutate(Year = as.integer(Year))




I tried use theme_minimal() and cubic-in-out ，shadow_wake toSmooth out animations and ghosting

ggplot(globalPop, aes(x = Old, y = Young, 
                      size = Population, 
                      colour = Country)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, 
             show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = country_colors) +
  scale_size(range = c(2, 12)) +
  labs(title = 'Year: {frame_time}', 
       x = '% Aged', 
       y = '% Young') +
  transition_time(Year) +       
  ease_aes('linear')  
ggplot(globalPop, aes(x = Old, y = Young, 
                      size = Population, 
                      colour = Country)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = country_colors) +
  scale_size(range = c(2, 12)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = 'Global Aging Trends | Year: {frame_time}', 
       subtitle = 'Movement shows decreasing youth and increasing aged population',
       x = 'Aged Population (%)', 
       y = 'Young Population (%)',
       caption = "Source: Global Population Dataset") +
  transition_time(Year) +       
  ease_aes('cubic-in-out') +
  shadow_wake(wake_length = 0.1, alpha = FALSE)








The animated bubble plot provides a clear visualization of the shifting demographic structures across various countries over several decades. By observing the movement of the bubbles, we can identify several key trends.
the most significant trend is the general movement from the top-left to the bottom-right of the graph. This trajectory represents a simultaneous decrease in the percentage of the young population and an increase in the proportion of the elderly. In my understanding, this is a visual representation of global population aging, driven by falling birth rates and improved medical care which extends life expectancy.




gg <- ggplot(globalPop, 
       aes(x = Old, 
           y = Young, 
           size = Population, 
           colour = Country)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = Population,
                 frame = Year),
             alpha = 0.7, 
             show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = country_colors) +
  scale_size(range = c(2, 12)) +
  labs(x = '% Aged', 
       y = '% Young')

ggplotly(gg)





the animation highlights the disparity between continents. While European and some Asian nations (represented by specific colors) move rapidly towards the “aged” corner, many developing nations remain in the “young” zone for a longer duration.



bp <- globalPop %>%
  plot_ly(x = ~Old, 
          y = ~Young, 
          size = ~Population, 
          color = ~Continent,
          sizes = c(2, 100),
          frame = ~Year, 
          text = ~Country, 
          hoverinfo = "text",
          type = 'scatter',
          mode = 'markers'
          ) %>%
  layout(showlegend = FALSE)
bp





In summary, this dynamic chart is far more effective than a static one because it captures the speed of change. It allows us to conclude that while aging is a universal phenomenon, the pace varies significantly between different economic regions, which is crucial for future policy planning.
